title: Two-Minute Math: Mathematical Explanations Using Animations https://blog.lboro.ac.uk/cmc/2026/10/05/two-minute-math-mathematical-explanations-using-animations/
author: Colin Foster
summary: Colin Foster, a professor of mathematics education at Loughborough University, describes his summer project of producing more than 160 short video explanations of mathematics at twominutemath.org. He argues that teachers repeat the same explanations every year and that this accumulated pedagogical content knowledge can now be captured as animations, because TikZ inside LaTeX can generate vector animations that are tiny in file size and quick to load. AI help with writing and debugging the code is what made the volume possible, and he says he could not have produced anywhere near so many videos without it. The videos are deliberately minimalist, informed by the LUMEN Curriculum design principles, the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, John Mason's Open University films and Dave Hewitt's canonical images. He proposes uses for students, teachers, trainee teachers and experienced teachers, and says he would play them without sound while adding his own explanation. A technical note describes the stop-motion pipeline using R, LuaLaTeX and FFmpeg.
points: Teachers repeat the same explanations each year, so turning a hard-won explanation into a short animation preserves pedagogical content knowledge in a reusable form.
TikZ in LaTeX produces vector animations with file sizes of kilobytes, which makes them fast to load on a phone or browser.
AI assistance with coding and debugging is what let a single author produce over 160 videos in one summer, though he avoids animating when it would be 'a hammer in search of a nail'.

The videos follow minimalist design principles drawn from the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and he suggests students use a self-explanation workflow with pausing and note-making to avoid passive viewing.
Foster would use the videos muted so he can pause and add his own explanation, and he suggests teams watch them together to discuss what to do differently as professional development.
quotes: As they gain experience, school mathematics teachers and university mathematics lecturers get very used to explaining the same things over and over again. Each year, a new set of eager (or not so eager) students appears, but the mathematics we teach hardly changes.

But although I have used LaTeX and TikZ for many years, I only recently realised how easy it is to use TikZ to generate animations. It is quite accessible, even if you don’t have previous experience of these languages.

Because the generated images are vectors, the animation file sizes are tiny – often just kilobytes, or a few megabytes, so they are very quick to download and watch in a web browser, on a computer or even on a phone.

Not all the videos use animations – I have tried to avoid being ‘a hammer in search of a nail’ – but many do. And I could not have produced anywhere near so many videos over such a timescale without AI help with the coding.

It is easy to engage passively with videos, whereas if students are pausing, rewatching parts, making notes and asking themselves questions, it is possible that more active engagement is happening that will lead to longer-term learning.
The discussion aspect might be more valuable than any of the individual videos produced.

More experienced teachers might use the videos with their students without the sound, pausing where necessary to support their own explanation and to invite discussion. I think that’s how I would use them myself.
